name: Jamal Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a pick station in an electronics warehouse, so I don't walk the aisles much. Little orange robots carry whole shelving pods to my station, a light shows which bin, and I grab the phone case or charger and drop it in a tote. On a good day I do about 300 items an hour, which is still under target. It's ten-hour shifts, four days a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being next to the robots. I watch the maintenance guys fix them and ask them questions on my break. What wears me out is standing in one square metre for ten hours with a screen counting every second. My cousin Tunde, who I share a flat with, says I'm already half robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the hype was overdone, but the robots in our building already work, so that part isn't hype. I'd post something like that, I talk about this stuff online a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good news. I'm halfway through an online course for maintenance technicians, and if things stay steady I can finish it and apply internally. I'm not worried about losing my job. I'm worried about being stuck at a pick station forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the course module by module, about five hours a week, and apply for the next maintenance trainee place in spring. I use an AI app every day to quiz me on basic electrics. I've got about four months of savings and I'd leave them alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. Steady is fine when you've got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the plan go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they hire maintenance people from outside with proper certificates and skip people like me. I left school early, so this course is the only thing I'll have on paper. I'd ask my manager, Ruth, straight out what they're looking for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lean towards unions, but your site doesn't have one. How does that sit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. A few of us have been talking about getting the union recognised, and I've been to two meetings in a pub car park. Even if I move up, the people at the pick stations deserve a voice.

say: I'd say the hype was overdone, but the **robots in our building** already work.
I'd post about it online, since I **talk about tech** there a lot.
think: A steady world lets me **finish my course** and apply for maintenance internally.
My real fear is being **stuck** at a pick station, not losing the job.
do: Study the technician course for **five hours a week** and apply for a spring trainee place.
Use an **AI quiz app** daily and leave four months of savings untouched.
feel: **Pretty good**, because he has a plan and time to follow it.
S0.quote: I'm not worried about losing my job. I'm worried about being stuck at a pick station forever.
fieldNote: He already works **beside robots** and sees them as a ladder, not a threat.
His main risk is outside hires with **certificates** he lacks.
He is quietly helping a **union recognition** push despite planning to move up.

steps.text: Study the maintenance technician course five hours a week
Apply for the spring maintenance trainee place
Practise electrics daily with the AI quiz app
Go to the union recognition meetings with pickers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to train people, not sack them. The company should put every picker who wants it through the robot maintenance course. I'd post that, and I'd say it to Ruth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pick station job would shrink slowly, because the robots get better at grabbing items. But more robots means more broken robots, and somebody has to fix them. I want that somebody to be me. The planning office would feel it first, because that's the thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed up the course and try to finish by summer instead of next year. I'd volunteer for every robot fault I can, even just resetting stuck pods. And I'd use AI to help me read the wiring diagrams, which still look like spaghetti to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, and a little guilty. I'd be fine, and lots of my mates wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ahmed, who's on the station next to me. He's fifty-two, he hates screens, and he has three kids. I'd try to get him to the union meetings at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said guilty. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the same robots that give me a career take Ahmed's job. I can't fix that on my own. That's why I keep going on about the union, it's the one thing I can do for people like him.

say: I'd say this is the moment to **train pickers**, not sack them.
I'd tell my manager Ruth to offer the **maintenance course** to everyone.
think: Picking **shrinks slowly**, but more robots need more people to fix them.
The **planning office** feels it first, because that's the thinking work.
do: Finish the course **by summer** instead of next year.
Volunteer to **reset stuck pods** and shadow the maintenance team.
feel: **Excited** about his chances and **guilty** about colleagues who lack them.
S1.quote: More robots means more broken robots, and somebody has to fix them. I want that somebody to be me.
fieldNote: He reads Steady Disruption as an **opening** for himself.
His guilt about his older colleague Ahmed drives his **union** activity.
He correctly places **office planning** work ahead of picking in line for AI.

steps.text: Finish the maintenance course by summer
Use AI to decode robot wiring diagrams
Bring Ahmed from the next station to union meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for millions of people, fast, like a basic income while everyone works out what's next. I'd post a lot. At work I'd tell people to save whatever they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028 means the AI can diagnose a robot fault better than me. Then by 2031 the robots fix each other, or near enough. My whole plan gets squeezed from both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still finish the course, because hands-on repair lasts until 2031 at least. I'd push savings from four months to six by cutting gaming and eating out. And I'd look at moving to where the new automated parks are, near the port, because that's where the repair work will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. I thought robot maintenance was the safe side, and maybe there isn't a safe side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tunde?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin Tunde his delivery van job is in trouble too, maybe sooner than mine. We'd sit up late working out who pays the rent if one of us goes. We'd be fine for a while, we're both careful with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're cutting back and planning a move. Does that still work after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's what scares me. After 2031 I don't know what I'd be. Maybe I'd use the AI itself to find something new, I trust it more than a careers adviser.

say: I'd call for a **basic income** while millions of people retrain.
I'd tell people at work to **save** whatever they can.
think: By 2028 AI **diagnoses faults** better than me, and by 2031 robots repair robots.
My **maintenance plan** gets squeezed from both sides.
do: Finish the course anyway, since **hands-on repair** lasts until about 2031.
Cut gaming and meals out to reach **six months** of savings.
Look for repair jobs at the **automated parks** near the port.
feel: **Shaken**, because the safe side he chose may not exist.
S2.quote: I thought robot maintenance was the safe side, and maybe there isn't a safe side.
fieldNote: Fast AGI **undercuts** the plan he's proudest of.
He still sees value in the **three-year gap** before hands-on robots.
He'd trust AI over a **careers adviser**, a sign of his daily use.

steps.text: Cut gaming and meals out to reach six months saved
Apply for repair jobs at the automated parks near the port
Campaign online for a basic income during the switch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd say start the training now, not when it lands. I'd post about it and I'd push Ruth to set up a proper apprenticeship at our site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'd have a few years as a technician, and hands-on repair robots wouldn't come until about 2034. Six good years as a robot technician is long enough to save properly and work out what comes after. That's a real runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the course this year, get the maintenance job, then start saving for a flat deposit. I'd ask the AI to map out which skills last longest, maybe electrical work or fitting solar panels. And I'd keep pushing for the union so the change gets negotiated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. Busy, more than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why solar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone has to climb on roofs and wire things in old buildings, and every building is different. A robot that does all that is a long way off, I think. I could be wrong, but it's a bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay in school, honestly. Then I'd tell him not to panic. I left school early and I still found something to learn, and that habit matters more than any one job.

say: I'd say five years means **start training now**, not when AGI lands.
I'd push for an **apprenticeship** at our site.
think: Robots for hands-on repair come around **2034**, giving me about six good years.
That's long enough to **save properly** and plan the next step.
do: Get the **maintenance job**, then add an electrical or solar qualification.
Ask the AI which **skills last longest**.
S3.quote: Six good years as a robot technician is long enough to save properly and work out what comes after.
fieldNote: Five years turns his plan into a **runway** with a second step.
He bets on **varied hands-on** work like solar installation lasting longest.
He values the **habit of learning** over any single job.

steps.text: Add an electrical or solar qualification after the course
Ask the AI which trade skills will last longest
Start saving for a flat deposit
Keep pushing for union recognition at the site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for everyone to land somewhere, if the government gets serious. I'd post about free training for adults, because most people my age can't pay for courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the good one for me. By 2039 I'd be forty, with ten years in maintenance and maybe a second trade. I'd see the robots coming the whole way and get out in front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan, slower and calmer: finish the course, get the maintenance job, then start an electrical qualification in year two. I'd keep using AI every day for study. I'd help the union drive at work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. With ten years' warning, I'd have the map before the trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you get too relaxed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Tunde says I always start strong and then drift. But I've stuck with this course for eight months, which is a record for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older guys like Ahmed, still. Ten years is a long time for me, but Ahmed would be sixty-two by then, and nobody hires a sixty-two-year-old as a new robot technician.

say: I'd say a decade is enough **if the government** gets serious.
I'd post about **free training** for adults who can't pay for courses.
think: This is the **best case** for me: ten years in maintenance by 2039.
I'd see robots coming the whole way and **get out in front**.
do: Finish the course, get the **maintenance job**, then start electrics in year two.
Keep studying with **AI every day** and help the union drive.
feel: **Good**, like having the map before the trip.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, I'd have the map before the trip.
fieldNote: A decade makes this his **most hopeful** scenario.
His risk is **drifting**, which his cousin Tunde has noticed before.
He keeps returning to **older colleagues** like Ahmed who lack his options.

steps.text: Start an electrical qualification in the second year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the only one where my plan doesn't have time to work. What would help is free technician courses for adults and a basic income while people retrain, so nobody has to choose between rent and learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the robots are like to work with. Robots aren't scary, they're clumsy. They drop phone cases and get stuck on a bit of tape. I'd rather learn how they work than pretend they're not coming.

headlineQuote: Robots aren't scary, they're clumsy. They drop phone cases and get stuck on a bit of tape.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old pick station worker** in an electronics warehouse already full of shelf-carrying robots.
He is studying online to become a **robot maintenance technician** and uses AI daily to learn.
He is **progressive** and helps a union drive, partly out of guilt for older colleagues like Ahmed.
He stays **calm** in a plateau or with ten years' warning, and turns **anxious** only if AGI comes by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his maintenance plan wouldn't have time to pay off.
whatWouldHelp: **Free technician courses** for adults and a basic income while people retrain.
